name: Cardarine (GW501516)
lead: Cardarine, also called GW501516, GW-1516 and Endurobol, is an experimental drug that selectively activates the PPAR-delta receptor, which regulates how muscle burns fatty acids. In looksmaxxing and bodybuilding circles it is used with the aim of getting leaner and building endurance for cardio and cutting phases, usually described as a fat-loss or leanmaxxing add-on rather than something that builds muscle.[1][4][5][6]

Ligand Pharmaceuticals and GlaxoSmithKline (GSK) developed it from the 1990s as a possible treatment for high cholesterol and metabolic disease, and GSK ended development in 2007 after animal studies reported cancer in several organs at high doses.[1][2][3][16] Small randomised trials in healthy volunteers and in people with obesity or dyslipidemia reported effects on triglycerides, HDL cholesterol and fat oxidation; none was designed to test body-composition or appearance outcomes in healthy people.[7][8][9][10] A 2008 mouse study from the Salk Institute drew wide attention by reporting that the drug, combined with exercise, boosted running endurance.[24]

Cardarine is not a hormone or a SARM, though it is sold and discussed beside them. The World Anti-Doping Agency prohibits it and warned in 2013 about its health risks, and it has no approved medical use anywhere.[1][26]

chain: Muscle shifts toward burning fatty acids

angle.text: Users take cardarine alongside dieting and cardio hoping for a lower body-fat percentage and better stamina, which show more definition in the face and body. Trials measured blood lipids and fat oxidation in volunteers rather than appearance, so the link to a leaner look rests on the metabolic mechanism and user reports.

infobox: Prohibited by WADA since 2009; warning issued 2013[1][26]
No approved use; scheduled in Australia (2018); unscheduled in US and UK[1]

paras: People who use cardarine describe it as a fat-loss and endurance aid for cutting, often listed with clenbuterol, growth hormone or other compounds in leanmaxxing plans.[4][5][6][21] Posters say the goal is a lean physique and sharper facial definition, sometimes quickly before a deadline; some are teenagers asking whether to start it.[4][5] These are user reports, and no published trial has tested cardarine for body-fat or facial-leanness outcomes in healthy people.

It is taken as an oral product and is usually described as an add-on to diet and cardio rather than a standalone approach; it is sold online as a supposed research chemical, and users compare it with SARMs even though it works on a different receptor.[1][26][20][23]

GW501516 is a selective agonist of PPAR-delta, a nuclear receptor that acts as a sensor of dietary lipids and regulates fatty acid and carbohydrate metabolism.[11] Wikipedia lists an affinity of about 1 nanomolar for PPAR-delta, with more than 1,000-fold selectivity over PPAR-alpha and PPAR-gamma.[1] In muscle cells it increases expression of genes for fatty-acid transport, beta-oxidation and mitochondrial respiration, and in animals it attenuated features of metabolic syndrome.[12][13] In rats it recruits the coactivator PGC-1alpha, and in obese rhesus monkeys it raised HDL and lowered VLDL.[1]

Because it was reported to mimic aspects of exercise signalling, reviews list PPAR-delta agonists among exercise mimetics.[14] Human muscle studies have also examined PPAR-delta and AMP kinase in lipid and glucose handling.[15]

A 2008 paper from Ronald Evans's laboratory at the Salk Institute, reported in Cell, tested GW1516 and the AMPK activator AICAR in mice. Salk's news release said GW1516 alone in sedentary mice lowered fatty acids and blood glucose but had no effect on exercise performance, while GW1516 combined with daily treadmill training improved endurance by 77 percent over training alone and raised slow-twitch muscle fibers by 38 percent; AICAR improved endurance in untrained mice by 44 percent.[24] The release stressed that the work was in mice and that the drug was investigational, and noted that the lead researcher worked with anti-doping officials on a detection test ahead of the 2008 Olympics.[24]

GSK carried the compound through phase I and II trials for dyslipidemia before stopping.[2][1] A randomized trial in healthy volunteers examined effects on triglycerides and HDL cholesterol.[7] A randomized, double-blind, crossover trial of six-week treatment periods tested GW501516 against placebo on lipoprotein metabolism in dyslipidemic men with central obesity.[8] A 2008 randomized trial in moderately obese men reported that PPAR-delta activation was associated with reversal of multiple metabolic abnormalities, less oxidative stress and increased fatty acid oxidation.[9] A trial in people with low HDL cholesterol and features of metabolic syndrome examined lipid effects.[10] A review notes that, after clinical trials in diabetes, GSK announced that research would stop because preclinical rodent studies linked the drug to widespread tumour development.[16]
None of these trials had body weight, body fat or physique in healthy people as its focus, and no study has tested the doses or durations described in looksmaxxing forums.

The main documented concern is cancer in animals. GSK is reported to have found rapid cancer development in multiple organs in mice and rats at a dose of 3 mg/kg per day, including liver, stomach, tongue, skin, bladder, ovaries, womb and testes, according to Wikipedia.[1] A mouse study found that activation of PPAR-delta accelerated intestinal adenoma growth,[17] and a 2018 mouse study linked GW501516 to faster growth of colitis-associated colorectal cancer.[1] A review of PPARbeta/delta agonists describes the tumour findings as the reason for GSK discontinuing research.[16] The US Anti-Doping Agency says the compound was pulled after it was found to cause cancer and urges athletes not to use it.[26] No long-term human safety data are available.

A 2024 case report described reversible gynecomastia and hypogonadism in a user of a commercial performance-enhancing supplement; the report concerns supplement products as a group and its relevance to cardarine specifically depends on the product's contents.[18]

Ligand and GSK collaborated from 1992 on PPAR compounds. According to Wikipedia, GSK began phase I trials in 2000 and a 2001 PNAS paper described GW501516 as a selective PPAR-delta agonist that promoted reverse cholesterol transport.[1][19] Phase I/II trials began in 2002, and a 2006 review described GSK and Ligand as developing it for dyslipidemia with phase II trials ongoing.[1][2] GSK dropped development in 2007, and later animal testing showed cancer.[1]

Concern about use by athletes emerged before the 2008 Beijing Olympics.[1][24] WADA prohibited it in 2009, and in March 2013 issued a health warning stating that clinical approval has not and will not be given for it.[1][26]

Wikipedia lists positive tests among cyclists in Costa Rica in 2012, Russian cyclist Valery Kaykov and Venezuelan Miguel Ubeto in 2013, Russian race walker Elena Lashmanova in 2014, US boxer Jarrell Miller in 2019, and sprinter Nijel Amos in 2022; in 2023 sprinter Issam Asinga attributed a positive test to contaminated gummies in a lawsuit.[1] USADA reported 31 sanctions related to the compound worldwide as of 2017 and says it is prohibited at all times under metabolic modulators.[26]

A 2017 JAMA study bought 44 products sold online as SARMs and tested them: 39 percent contained another unapproved drug, including GW501516, and only 41 percent contained the labeled amount of active compound.[25] GW501516 was the second most frequently detected compound after the SARMs ostarine and LGD-4033, and it was listed on several labels.[25] USADA warns supplements may be contaminated with it and notes sellers label it a research chemical.[26]

Cardarine is unapproved as a drug. Australia scheduled it as illegal in 2018, while the US and UK list it as unscheduled.[1] Natural bodybuilding organisations list it among prohibited substances.[20]

On looksmax.org, cardarine appears in threads from teenagers and young men planning to lose fat quickly, in comparisons with clenbuterol, and in combinations with HGH and other compounds.[4][5][6][21][22] One thread title argues that anyone not taking cardarine while leanmaxxing is "not even trying."[22] A reply to a 17-year-old asking about it jokingly renamed it "Cancerine," and the poster mentions semaglutide or retatrutide as later plans.[4] On T Nation, it is listed in multi-SARM stacks and cycles.[20][23]

lore.intro: Cardarine is discussed on looksmax.org as a fat-loss and endurance add-on for leanmaxxing, often alongside other drugs, with recurring jokes and warnings about cancer [4][22].

claims.claim: Cardarine helps you get lean quickly
claims.believers: Posters planning cuts, including teenagers, say they intend to use it alone or with diet; a title argues it is essential to leanmaxxing [4][21][22].
claims.experts: Small randomized trials report improved triglycerides, HDL and fatty acid oxidation in volunteers with dyslipidemia or obesity, but fat loss in healthy people has not been the studied outcome [7][8][9].

claims.claim: It is a milder option than clenbuterol
claims.believers: A looksmax.org user said clenbuterol side effects are bad and GW is better, while noting that clenbuterol is stronger [6].
Forum users joke about "Cancerine" and warn about risk [4].
claims.experts: GSK stopped development after rodent studies linked the drug to widespread tumours, and a mouse study linked PPAR-delta activation to faster adenoma growth; no human cancer data exist [16][17][1].

claims.believers: It is marketed as Endurobol and discussed as an endurance aid.
claims.experts: Large performance gains were reported in mice at high doses; human endurance trials have not been reported. WADA prohibits it as performance enhancing [1].

claims.claim: It is only an endurance drug and is not a SARM
claims.believers: Posters often group it with SARMs in stacks and cycles.[20][23]
claims.experts: USADA says it is actually a PPAR-delta agonist, and the 2017 JAMA authors note it is not a SARM.[26][25]

claims.claim: Products sold as cardarine or SARMs contain what the label says
claims.believers: Sellers label products as research chemicals or supplements.[26]
claims.experts: A 2017 JAMA analysis of 44 online products found only 41 percent contained the labeled amount of the active compound.[25]

claims.claim: Exercise-mimetic effect lets it replace training
claims.believers: The Endurobol nickname reflects the idea of endurance without effort.[1]
claims.experts: Salk reported that GW1516 alone had no effect on mouse exercise performance and improved endurance only with training.[24]

card.summary: A discontinued metabolic drug sold as a fat-loss and endurance aid; some lipid benefits in small trials, but rodent cancer findings ended its development.
card.note: Rodent studies found cancer in several organs; banned in sport; no approved use.

quick.overview:
Cardarine is an experimental drug that activates PPAR-delta, a receptor that turns up fat burning in muscle. GSK developed it for cholesterol and metabolic disease and then stopped in 2007.

Small human trials showed better triglycerides, HDL and fat oxidation, but none was designed to test weight or fat loss in healthy people. It is sold alongside SARMs and used by some in cuts.
quick.mechanism: It selectively activates PPAR-delta, which raises expression of genes for fatty acid transport and oxidation in muscle and has been described as mimicking some effects of exercise.
quick.risks: Rodent studies found tumour development in several organs, which led GSK to halt research. There are no long-term human safety data. It is banned by WADA and unapproved, and some countries such as Australia have scheduled it.
